messages.body_plain:

I have a F1 progeny from two outbred parents (4way cross then) with no missing genotype information and with around 600 markers. R propose 4 methods for interval mapping (em, imp, haley-knott and extended haley-knott)

I wanted to know if I should do the QTL detection with the EM method proposed in R or if another method would fit better than this one for my case. I thought about the multiple imputation method but as I don't have missing genotyping data, I am not sure I need it.
Furthermore, i would like to perform after that a QTL detection with Multiple QTL Mapping and i read that "multiple imputation (imp method) has greatest value for the fit and exploration of MQM models". So I am a little lost in the choice of the method for the first step of my qtl detection.

 Could you give any advice according your experience ? How do/did you do to choose between the method ?
This would really help me because i would like to understand the way that scientists choose their method so I can make a reasonable and thoughful decision for my analysis.

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
For a detailed discussion of the relative advantage of the different methods for handling missing data, see chapter 4 of the R/qtl book (https://rqtl.org/book).

In a typical 4-way cross, many markers would be less-than-fully informative. It's hard to know, from the information you've provided, whether 600 markers is a lot or not, and it partly depends on how they are distributed across the genome. Are there any regions with gaps. plotInfo() can be useful for assessing the amount of missing genotype information.

If you're interested in fitting multiple-QTL models, you might start with the multiple imputation approach. With more imputations [n.draws in sim.geno()] everything takes more time and memory but does a better job of dealing with missing genotype information. If you repeat analyses (sim.geno and then scanone) and get rather different results, you likely need to increase n.draws.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I just saw the same discussion on github

https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/issues/9

here the suggestion is

"Just give the same row repeated, with marker names as column names.
It's possible to estimate sex-specific maps with 4-way crosses, in which case Female would go in the first row and male in the second."

So I did this hack in my code:

threatment=read.cross("csvr",".","Threatment_12x52-order_wp_lodlimit-20_js_sexAveraged.txt.rqtlCrossFormat.csvr",skip=1,genotypes=NULL,crosstype="4way")

for(i in 1:length(threatment$geno))
{
  a=as.matrix(threatment$geno[[i]]$map)
  threatment$geno[[i]]$map=t(cbind(a,a[,1]))
}
summary(threatment)
threatment<-calc.genoprob(threatment,step=1)

messages.subject_clean: Singular matrix error in mqmscan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to do an mqmscan with an F2 cross, 112 individuals with 3192 markers distributed across 49 linkage groups. I have two questions regarding this process.

The first concerns the mqmaugmentdata method of filling in missing data. The function is taking a very long time to run on a cluster, probably because of the large number of markers. Is it likely to finish in a reasonable amount of time with such a large dataset? Even a couple of weeks is fine.

The second question concerns the singular matrix error that many other people have run into in this group. When using fill.geno to simulate missing data, mqmscan gives the error, Singular Matrix. Following some advice posted in another discussion, I've tried to isolate the linkage group responsible for the error. While no one linkage group is causing the failure, it seems that any combination of linkage groups containing about 1500 markers will produce the singular matrix error. Combinations containing less than 1400 markers consistently work with mqmscan. This seems to suggest the the problem is either caused by too many markers or too much map distance. Are there any suggestions with how to resolve this error? There are definitely duplicate markers in the map, but those don't seem to cause a problem if I artificially trim the dataset.

I have successfully mapped my QTL with scanone, and stepwiseqtl, but it would be nice to further validate those results with mqmscan.

Thanks,
Tyler

messages.body_plain:
stepwiseqtl() is seeking the model that optimizes the penalized LOD score, but its search method won't necessarily that find the globally optimal model. And in this case there's an added source of variability, as you've re-run the imputations from sim.geno, and 200 imputations is not sufficient here.

You're treating the cross as "4way" but with markers segregating on just one side? That's not going to work for this analysis. You're fitting a 3 parameters for each QTL and an additional 9 parameters for each QTL:QTL interaction, but you've got information only about the genotype on one chromosome at each QTL.

Also, others have reported that stepwiseqtl() doesn't work properly for cross type "4way", though to be honest I can't remember the nature of the problem.

karl

messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't suggest using _only_ the markers that are segregating in both parents. But if you want to do QTL analysis with cross type "4way", you'll need some way to integrate the full set of markers. But unfortunately you'd probably need to do more work to identify and genotype additional markers that allow you to integrate the markers.

It's possible that stepwiseqtl() can work with a 4-way cross, but some users have reported errors and we've not been able to track them down and fix them.

Working with markers segregating in one parent and treating it as a backcross is one way to try to do QTL analysis with your data, but I'm not sure that I would recommend it. Certainly you'll need to proceed with caution.

karl

messages.body_plain:
est.rf() looks at each pair of markers in isolation and seeks to estimate the recombination fraction between them.
In a backcross, it seems counts recombination events.
In an intercross, it needs to use an interative algorithm to deal with the het:het cases (which could be 0 or 2 recombinations).
In either case, any individual with a missing genotype at one or the other marker is omitted.

est.map() considers all the markers on a chromosome, one chromosome at a time, and uses a hidden Markov model to estimate the inter-marker distances, jointly. It uses data on all individuals including those with missing genotypes, and uses a model that accommodates genotyping error.

karl

Yes, the intervals take the regions where the LOD score is within 1.5 of the peak and then turn them into a single connected interval. So if the LOD goes down a bit and then back up, you’ll get the wider interval. I would stick with this rather than exclude the larger region.

I think the reason interval ends up dropping 4 and 8 in LOD is that we calculate the endpoints only at discrete positions, and the LOD scores I likely dropping rapidly. Check that if you move one pseudomarker interior, you get LOD difference from the maximum of < 1.5.

karl
